components.title: The Water Cycle
components.subtitle: Understanding Earth's continuous journey of water

components.title: How Water Moves Through Earth's Systems
components.dek: Water perpetually cycles through evaporation, condensation, and precipitation.
components.hook: Water is never created or destroyed on Earth—it simply transforms and moves between the atmosphere, land, and oceans in a continuous cycle powered by the sun.
components.model: Think of it as a cosmic recycling system where the sun acts as the pump.
components.model_note: Every water molecule that falls as rain today may have once been in an ancient ocean or dinosaur.
components.closing_note: The water cycle is a closed system—the total amount of water on Earth stays roughly constant, but its location and form are always changing.

components.label: EVAPORATION
components.title: Water Rises as Vapor
components.body: The sun's heat transforms liquid water from oceans, lakes, and rivers into invisible water vapor. This invisible gas rises into the atmosphere, carrying water molecules skyward. Plants also release water through transpiration, combining with evaporation to form evapotranspiration.
components.code_caption: Energy from the sun drives the phase change

components.label: CONDENSATION
components.title: Vapor Becomes Visible
components.body: As water vapor rises into the cooler upper atmosphere, it cools and condenses into liquid water droplets around microscopic dust particles. Billions of these droplets cluster together to form clouds—the visible sign that water has changed form again.
components.code: Water Vapor + Cooling → Liquid Droplets → Clouds
components.code_caption: Clouds are collections of trillions of tiny water droplets

components.label: PRECIPITATION
components.title: Water Returns to Earth
components.body: When cloud droplets combine and become too heavy, they fall back to Earth as precipitation: rain, snow, sleet, or hail. This water lands on mountains, forests, plains, and oceans—completing a cycle that takes days, years, or even millennia.
components.code_caption: Precipitation is the only way water returns from clouds to the surface

components.label: WORKED EXAMPLE
components.title: Tracking One Water Droplet's Journey
components.body: Imagine a raindrop lands in the Atlantic Ocean on Monday. Over the next week, solar radiation heats the ocean surface, and our droplet evaporates into water vapor. The vapor rises 3,000 meters into the atmosphere, where temperatures plummet. Our droplet condenses into a cloud droplet over the Azores. By Friday, the cloud drifts over Portugal and cools further. Our droplet combines with others and falls as rain on a hillside. Some of this water soaks into soil (infiltration), where it may be absorbed by tree roots and later transpired back into the air, or it may percolate deep underground to become groundwater.
components.code: Ocean → Evaporation → Rise → Condensation → Cloud → Precipitation → Land → Infiltration → Groundwater
components.takeaway: A single water molecule can take different paths: some cycles last days, others take thousands of years.

components.question: What is the primary energy source that drives the water cycle?
options: Earth's internal heat from the core
components.explanation: The sun provides the energy that evaporates water from oceans and land surfaces, making it the engine of the entire water cycle.

components.question: Which process describes water vapor cooling and turning into liquid water droplets?
components.explanation: Condensation is the phase change from gas (water vapor) to liquid. This occurs in the upper atmosphere where temperatures are much cooler.

components.question: How does water return from clouds back to Earth's surface?
options: Through sublimation directly into the ground
Through precipitation such as rain, snow, or hail
Through absorption by the ozone layer
components.explanation: Precipitation is the only mechanism by which water from clouds returns to the surface. When water droplets become too heavy, gravity pulls them down as rain, snow, sleet, or hail.
